CHAPTER 5: THE TEACHINGS OF JESUS AND THEIR IMPACT ON THE COMMUNITY (Section B: Christianity - Origins and Contemporary Expressions)

BIG IDEA
- To understand Jesus' teaching we must understand the Jewish beliefs of the first century: the prophetic tradition, eschatology, apocalypticism and metanoia.
- At the heart of Jesus' teaching was the Kingdom of God - God's presence among people.
- Jesus revealed the Kingdom through his parables, his meals, his miracles and his prayer, with a sense of urgency.
- "The message and the man are one" - we cannot separate Jesus' teaching from the life he lived.
- Opening quote, Mahatma Gandhi: "We must be the change we wish to see in the world."

KEY TERMS
- Eschatology: concern with the "end of time" and "last things" - judgement, heaven, hell and the ultimate meaning of life.
- Apocalypticism: a focus on the coming end ("the end is nigh"), God's future and final judgement, and the dawning of a new age or aeon.
- Metanoia: the call for immediate repentance and conversion (a change of heart).
- Kingdom of God: God's reign and presence among people; at the centre of Jesus' preaching - inclusive, forgiving, loving and just.
- Parable: a story drawn from ordinary, everyday life, with a religious or moral lesson conveyed indirectly, intended to convince or persuade, to bring the hearer to decision or action.
- Sermon on the Mount: Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5:1-12 (the section on what to expect in the Kingdom of God), which reveals his vision of the kingdom.
- Abba: an intimate word for father, most accurately translated as "Dada"; Jesus' name for God.
- Miracles: the great deeds of Jesus - extraordinary happenings and cures - that announce the Kingdom of God.

THE TEACHINGS OF JESUS IN CONTEXT - HOW THE GROUPS SAW THE KINGDOM
- The term "Kingdom of God" was not frequently used at the time.
- Zealots: expected a political king who would banish the Romans by force and restore Israel to the chosen people.
- Sadducees: hoped for deliverance but saw the Temple and their priestly function as important.
- Pharisees: strict adherence to the Law was what mattered most for the survival of God's people.
- Essenes: separated from society and awaited the "new age" that would come with the Messiah.

WHAT UNITED AND DIVIDED THE JEWISH GROUPS
- United: belief in the one true God who had chosen the people of Israel.
- Divided by:
- Their interpretation of the scriptures, especially the Law.
- Their attitude to the problem of human suffering and unhappiness.
- Their understanding of God's presence in history and their beliefs about the end of time.

THE PROPHETIC TRADITION
- Prophets emerged at particular times; claimed a special calling from God and a special function in Jewish history.
- They commented on the moral and ethical life of the people, called them to repentance, and identified dangers to religious life.
- Preached repentance, conversion and obedience to God's law.
- Failure to respond would be punished severely by God's judgement at the end of time.
- This concern with the end of time is eschatology ("last things": judgement, heaven, hell, ultimate meaning of life).

APOCALYPTICISM
- Every age, including ours, is concerned with the end of the world; it is human to wonder how we got here, why we are here and how we leave.
- Some groups at the time of Jesus were preoccupied with "the end" - "the end is nigh".
- The warning gave people a chance to mend their ways and make peace with God before it was too late.
- Concern: God's future and final judgement and the dawning of a new age or aeon.
- All Jewish groups were familiar with apocalyptic ideas and had a view on the "crisis" of the age.
- Because of the turbulence of the time, there was a heightened expectation that God would intervene decisively and save the suffering people, and the Kingdom of God would bring a new age.
- Radical apocalypticists had given up on their own age and pinned their hopes on the new age; this affected how they lived, their belief in God and their morals.

METANOIA
- In an apocalyptic context, the expectation of the end and the need for repentance and conversion went hand in hand.
- The call for immediate repentance and conversion is metanoia.
- Found throughout the Bible and Torah: made by ancient prophets to keep Israel faithful; by those who believed God's judgement was near; by rabbis and teachers protecting people from pagan and "foreign" influence.
- Associated with apocalyptic literature but not only with it.
- Jesus also called for metanoia in his preaching about the Kingdom of God.

JESUS - TEACHER, PREACHER, RABBI
- Jesus was a Jew, born into the complex and tense world of Galilee.
- Began his public ministry as a teacher, preacher and wandering rabbi.
- His relationship with John the Baptist was significant: he had been a disciple of John, then returned to Galilee and began preaching.
- Jesus belongs in the Prophetic tradition: he critiqued the behaviour and organisation of God's people and called them to look into their hearts and mend their ways.
- He interpreted the scriptures to teach and preach.
- He challenged the values of his day - individuals, groups and those in power - to re-evaluate their behaviour and relationship with God.
- At the heart of his teaching: a message about God and God's presence among people - the Kingdom of God.
- He invited people to re-imagine their relationship with God and raised questions: How is God present? What is God's will and how is it discerned? What is the place of the Law?
- "The message and the man are one" - so we look at the people around Jesus, his stories, the meals he shared and the things he did.

THE KINGDOM OF GOD IN PARABLES
- Jesus did not invent the parable; parables, proverbs and storytelling were common in the Near East, especially among the Jews.
- Philosophers such as Plato and Socrates used parables.
- Parables appear in the oldest books of the Bible, e.g. the parable of the lamb told by Nathan to David (2 Samuel 12:1-4).
- Modern definition: stories drawn from ordinary, everyday life, with a religious or moral lesson conveyed indirectly, intended to convince or persuade, to bring the hearer to decision or action.
- A parable draws on the lived experience of listeners, seeks a change in thinking, and asks them to question their behaviour.
- Jesus was a master of the parable. He gave value to the experience of his listeners and so to the ordinary, "unimportant" members of society.
- Characters: fathers and sons, brides and bridegrooms, women cleaning houses or carrying water, farmers, shepherds, vineyard workers, masters and servants.
- Listeners: rich, poor, widowed, sick, pious and marginalised; they could see themselves in the stories.
- Parables caught listeners unawares and surprised them; presented an alternative view of the world; called them to renew their covenant with God and showed another way to live.
- The unexpected happens:
- The faithful son goes unrewarded (Luke 15:11-32 - the Lost Son).
- The careful servant is admonished (Matthew 25:14-27).
- Those who work one hour get the same pay as those who work all day (Matthew 20:1-16 - Workers in the Vineyard).
- The least among us is the greatest (Luke 18:9-14).
- In his parables Jesus calls listeners to metanoia.
- He invited people to choose peace over violence, include rather than exclude, share rather than hoard, and know God as a loving God - these are the characteristics of the Kingdom.
- The Kingdom is a place where the sick are healed and the poor cared for - a place of justice, compassion and forgiveness.
- "The last will be first, and the first will be last" (Matthew 20:16).
- Other parables listed: the Lost Sheep (Matthew 18:10-14), the Great Feast (Luke 14:15-24), the Rich Fool.
- Matthew 5:1-12 (Sermon on the Mount): not a parable, but Jesus tells people what to expect in the Kingdom; it reveals his vision of the kingdom.

THE KINGDOM OF GOD IN THE MEALS OF JESUS
- Story of the banquet of huge forks: in hell people cannot feed themselves; in heaven people feed each other.
- Sr Consilio on Cuan Mhuire: "We live as a family at Cuan Mhuire. The people who make the best recovery are the ones who respect and watch out for others..." People leave as better persons, having discovered their own inner goodness.
- The gospels have many accounts of Jesus sharing meals; who he ate with and what he said and did reveal both the person and the message.
- Sometimes he scandalised religious people by his choice of company; other times he used meals to teach his vision for the future.
- Christians today remember Jesus and worship God through the Eucharist - a sacred meal remembering the Last Supper.
- Accounts of the Last Supper are in all four gospels; Jesus asked his followers to remember him, especially in the breaking of bread.
- In John's gospel, before eating, Jesus washed his followers' feet as a sign that service is the way of the Lord, and asked them to do this in memory of him (John 13:1-20).
- Jesus' vision: a future where God reigns; the Kingdom would be inclusive, forgiving, loving, just - where the poor and sick find peace.
- Jesus called God "Abba", a term of intimacy and closeness; God is loving and caring with unlimited capacity to forgive those who truly seek it.
- Meals with outcasts:
- Ate with tax collectors and sinners (Matthew 9:10-13).
- Ate with Simon the leper (Matthew 26:6-13; Mark 14:3-9).
- At a Pharisee's house met "a woman in the city who was a sinner" (Luke 7:36-50).
- He went out of his way to be with the excluded and despised; all were welcome at God's table.
- After the Resurrection he revealed himself in sharing food (John 21:1-14; Luke 24:13-35 - the road to Emmaus).
- In his vision the poor, orphan, widow and sick share equally in God's blessings; the fractured, divided people of God would be united as one.
- The Temple and its priests represented official Judaism; the Temple collected taxes and was partly an economic institution.
- Jesus challenged structures that made people pay for access to God's blessing, and challenged the accepted link between wealth and God's blessing.
- This is why people of power and prestige were nervous of him - a hint of what happened in his last days in Jerusalem.

THE KINGDOM OF GOD IN THE MIRACLES OF JESUS
- Jesus was an inspired preacher; people were drawn to him. He announced the Kingdom most powerfully through his great deeds - miracles.
- In biblical times illness was seen as punishment for sin (perhaps the parents' sin) and a sign of God's displeasure.
- Healing miracles show God cares for those who suffer:
- A blind man sees (Matthew 9:27-30).
- A leper is cured (Matthew 8:1-3).
- A woman bent low stands erect (Luke 13:11-13).
- The Kingdom: the blind see, the sick are cured, those on the edge are included; God loves all people and God's will triumphs over evil and sin; through Jesus the Covenant is renewed.
- Other miracles show:
- Plenty for all - loaves and fishes (Matthew 14:13-21).
- No need to be afraid - calming of the storm (Luke 8:22-25).
- Death has no power over God - raising of Lazarus (John 11:1-44) and Jairus' daughter (Luke 8:40-56).
- All - men and women, sick, needy, those on the edge - welcomed by a loving, just God.
- The gospel writers wanted to reassure the young, vulnerable Church that Jesus would always be with them. The miracles reminded followers how special Jesus was and that God spoke through him and continued to through the early Church.

THE KINGDOM OF GOD IN THE PRAYERS OF JESUS
- Jesus was a devout Jew, familiar with the Torah, observing Jewish custom and law.
- At times he reinterpreted the Law and named its heart: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the greatest and first commandment." (Matthew 22:37-38)
- He claimed a very special, intimate relationship with God, seen in the word "Abba" ("Dada"), a term of love and trust. Every use of it was in effect a prayer.
- He proclaimed a God who is loving, caring, understanding and always present - not distant, harsh or judgemental.
- The prayer most associated with Jesus is the one he taught his followers - the Lord's Prayer (Luke 11:1-4).

A SENSE OF URGENCY
- Many parables call hearers to act now and change their lives immediately; linked to the coming of the Kingdom.
- The ten maidens (Matthew 25:1-13): be ready, for we know not the hour the bridegroom will come.
- The unfaithful servant caught unawares by his master's return (Matthew 24:45-51).
- Jesus said to be always ready for the future coming of the Kingdom - and also that the Kingdom had already come in him.
- Mark 1:14-15: after John was arrested, Jesus came to Galilee proclaiming: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near; repent, and believe in the good news." (Also Matthew 4:12-17; Luke 4:16-21.)
- Jesus lived and preached a world where mercy ruled justice, the despised were loved and love of God was the centre of life; he gave people a glimpse of God's kingdom and showed how they could make it possible.

SUMMARY - CHARACTERISTICS OF THE KINGDOM OF GOD
- Inclusive (all welcome at God's table; outcasts included).
- Forgiving and loving (Abba; unlimited forgiveness).
- Just and compassionate (poor cared for, sick healed; last first).
- Peaceful (peace over violence; sharing not hoarding).
- Both present now in Jesus and still to come (urgency, be ready).

rows.prompt: Explain in your own words the difference between eschatology and apocalypticism.
rows.model_answer: Eschatology is a concern with the end of time and 'last things' - judgement, heaven, hell and the meaning of life. Apocalypticism is a strong focus on the end coming soon - 'the end is nigh' - and on God's final judgement and the dawn of a new age.

rows.prompt: Name the three things that divided the Jewish groups of Jesus' time.
rows.model_answer: Their interpretation of the scriptures, especially the Law. Their attitude to the problem of human suffering and unhappiness. Their understanding of God's presence in history and their beliefs about the end of time.

rows.prompt: Explain what is meant by metanoia and who called for it.
rows.model_answer: Metanoia is the call for immediate repentance and conversion. It was made by the ancient prophets, by those who believed God's judgement was near, and by rabbis protecting people from pagan influence. Jesus also called for metanoia when preaching the Kingdom of God, especially through his parables.

rows.prompt: Why were Jesus' parables so effective with his listeners?
rows.model_answer: They drew on everyday life - farmers, shepherds, fathers and sons - so listeners could see themselves in the stories. They caught people unawares with surprising endings and presented another view of the world. This challenged listeners to question their behaviour and change their lives.

rows.prompt: Name two meals Jesus shared and say what each reveals about the Kingdom of God.
rows.model_answer: Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners (Matthew 9:10-13), showing that all are welcome at God's table, even the despised. At the Last Supper he washed his followers' feet (John 13:1-20), showing that service is the way of the Lord.

rows.prompt: What do Jesus' healing miracles reveal about the Kingdom of God?

rows.prompt: Explain the significance of Jesus calling God 'Abba'.

rows.prompt: Explain the sense of urgency in Jesus' preaching about the Kingdom of God.
rows.model_answer: Many parables call people to act now and change immediately, like the ten maidens who must be ready for the bridegroom. Jesus said 'The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near; repent' (Mark 1:15). The Kingdom was still to come but had also already come in him.

rows.prompt: Write a brief note on eschatology and apocalypticism as understood by the Jewish people at the time of Jesus.
rows.model_answer:
Eschatology is the concern with the 'end of time' and 'last things' - judgement, heaven, hell and the ultimate meaning of life. In the prophetic tradition, prophets claimed a special calling from God. They commented on the moral life of the people and preached repentance, conversion and obedience to God's law, warning that failure to respond would be punished severely by God's judgement at the end of time.

Apocalypticism was a particular focus on 'the end', with the message 'the end is nigh'. The warning gave people a chance to mend their ways and make peace with God before it was too late. It looked to God's final judgement and the dawning of a new age. All Jewish groups knew these ideas, and because of the turbulence of Roman rule there was a heightened expectation that God would intervene decisively to save the suffering people and that the Kingdom of God would bring a new age. Radical apocalypticists had given up on their own age altogether. This affected how they lived, and it went hand in hand with metanoia - the call for immediate repentance and conversion.

rows.prompt: Describe the Kingdom of God as preached by Jesus in his parables. Refer to at least two parables in your answer.
rows.model_answer:
A parable is a story drawn from everyday life, with a religious or moral lesson conveyed indirectly, meant to bring the hearer to decision or action. Jesus did not invent parables - Nathan told David a parable - but he was a master of them. His stories used farmers, shepherds, fathers and sons, and servants, so ordinary people could see themselves in them. This gave value to the 'unimportant' members of society.

Jesus' parables often caught listeners unawares with an unexpected twist, presenting an alternative view of the world. In the Workers in the Vineyard (Matthew 20:1-16), those who worked for one hour received the same pay as those who worked all day. This shows that God's generosity is not earned, and that in the Kingdom 'the last will be first, and the first will be last'. In the Lost Son (Luke 15:11-32), the faithful son goes unrewarded, which surprised listeners and challenged their idea of who deserves God's love.

Through the parables Jesus invited people to choose peace over violence, to include rather than exclude, to share rather than hoard, and to know God as loving. The Kingdom is a place where the sick are healed and the poor cared for - of justice, compassion and forgiveness. Parables like the ten maidens (Matthew 25:1-13) add urgency: people must change now - metanoia.

May refer to: everyday life; Nathan; master of parables; value to ordinary people; surprise; Workers in the Vineyard; Lost Son; Lost Sheep; Great Feast; careful servant; Luke 18:9-14; peace, inclusion, sharing, loving God; justice, compassion, forgiveness; last first; urgency; metanoia.

rows.prompt: 'The meals Jesus shared revealed his vision of the Kingdom of God.' Discuss this statement with reference to the gospels.
rows.model_answer:
The people Jesus ate with, and what he said and did at meals, give insight into both the person of Jesus and his message. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners (Matthew 9:10-13) and with Simon the leper (Matthew 26:6-13). At a Pharisee's house he met a 'woman in the city who was a sinner' (Luke 7:36-50). He sometimes scandalised religious people by his choice of company, going out of his way to be with the excluded and despised. This showed that all are welcome at God's table.

At the Last Supper, found in all four gospels, Jesus asked his followers to remember him in the breaking of bread. In John's gospel he washed their feet as a sign that service is the way of the Lord (John 13:1-20). Christians today remember this in the Eucharist. After the Resurrection he revealed himself in sharing food, as on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:13-35).

These meals show a Kingdom that is inclusive, forgiving, loving and just, where the poor and the sick find peace and God is a loving 'Abba'. Jesus also challenged the Temple's link between wealth and God's blessing by eating with the poorest of the poor. This explains why people of power became nervous of him.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: tax collectors and sinners; Simon the leper; sinful woman at Pharisee's house; scandal; all welcome at God's table; Last Supper, remember me, breaking of bread; foot-washing, service; Eucharist; post-Resurrection meals (John 21, Emmaus); inclusive, forgiving, loving, just Kingdom; Abba; challenge to wealth/Temple; reaction of powerful.

rows.prompt: Outline what the miracles of Jesus reveal about his vision of the Kingdom of God.
rows.model_answer:
Jesus announced the Kingdom of God most powerfully through his great deeds, or miracles. In biblical times illness was seen as a punishment for sin and a sign of God's displeasure. When Jesus enabled a blind man to see (Matthew 9:27-30), cured a leper (Matthew 8:1-3) and helped a woman bent low to stand erect (Luke 13:11-13), he showed that God cares for those who suffer. The Kingdom is a place where the blind see, the sick are cured and those on the edge of society are included.

Other miracles show more about the Kingdom. The loaves and fishes (Matthew 14:13-21) show there is plenty for all. The calming of the storm (Luke 8:22-25) shows there is no need to be afraid. The raising of Lazarus (John 11:1-44) and of Jairus' daughter show that death has no power over God. The gospel writers also wanted to reassure the young, vulnerable Church that Jesus would always be with them.
